text: In Slack's API every channel-like thing is a conversation: public channel, private channel, DM (is_im) or multi-person DM (is_mpim). conversations.open opens or resumes a DM and returns its channel ID; chat.postMessage can also take a user ID and opens the DM if needed.
why: Confirms the DM-as-channel model from Slack's own API, with the exact type flags.

text: Slack exposes exactly this checkpoint: the conversation object's last_read is 'the timestamp for the last message the calling user has read in this channel', and conversations.mark moves that read cursor to a given message ts.
why: Shows the membership checkpoint is a real production design, at message-timestamp granularity.

text: If you do keep two either/or columns, the database can still forbid orphan rows: PostgreSQL's num_nonnulls() lets a CHECK constraint require exactly one of channel_id and receiver_id to be set.
why: Gives the precise fix for the orphan-row problem, so readers judge the trade-off correctly.

text: Slack has used MySQL for all its data from the beginning, originally partitioned by workspace id. From 2017 it migrated to Vitess (sharded MySQL), which by 2020 served 99% of its query load at about 2.3 million queries per second at peak.
why: Real-world evidence that sharded relational storage is enough for Slack.

text: Slack's original sharding by workspace kept each workspace on one shard. In moving to Vitess the team wanted to shard message data by channel id to spread load more evenly, the same key the lecture uses.
why: Connects the lecture's channel_id shard key to Slack's own choice and motivation.

text: Discord stored its messages in Cassandra (12 nodes and billions of messages in 2017) and moved them to ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database, in May 2022. Messages are partitioned by channel and a time bucket.
why: A public example of the high-ingestion consumer-chat choice the teacher describes.

text: With Cassandra the schema does change shape: modelling is query-driven, joins are not supported, and data is denormalised into one table per query, with a partition key that decides which node holds the data.
why: Stops readers from assuming a normalised relational schema carries over to Cassandra unchanged.

text: Browsers count WebSockets separately from ordinary HTTP connections. Chromium allows 6 normal sockets per host but 255 WebSockets per host ('WebSocket connections are long-lived, and should be treated differently'), and Firefox's network.websocket.max-connections is 200.
why: Corrects the 'one WebSocket eats one of six slots' model with the actual browser limits.

text: HTTP/2 runs many concurrent streams over a single connection, so on HTTP/2 sites the six-per-host cap does not throttle requests. RFC 8441 also lets a WebSocket run over a single stream of an HTTP/2 connection.
why: Explains why the HTTP/1.1 connection cap matters much less today.

text: Redis Pub/Sub delivery is at-most-once: if a subscriber errors or disconnects, the message is lost forever. When a missed message matters, Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery.
why: Names the delivery guarantee and the Redis alternative when persistence is needed.

text: Since Redis 7.0, sharded Pub/Sub (SSUBSCRIBE/SPUBLISH) assigns channels to cluster slots like keys and keeps each message within its shard. Classic PUBLISH in a cluster goes to every node, so only sharded Pub/Sub scales horizontally by adding shards.
why: Tells readers which Redis feature makes the 'cluster of Redis' actually scale.

text: This is what Socket.IO's Redis adapter does: it broadcasts packets between multiple Socket.IO servers through Redis Pub/Sub (a sharded variant needs Redis 7.0+). The adapter does not sign, encrypt or authenticate these messages, so Redis must stay inside trusted infrastructure.
why: Links the design to an off-the-shelf implementation and its security caveat.

text: Slack's published architecture differs in detail: in-memory Channel Servers own channels via consistent hashing (millions of channels per host), and Gateway Servers hold users' WebSocket subscriptions and subscribe to those Channel Servers. Slack reports delivering messages across the world in about 500 ms.
why: Lets readers compare the lecture design with how Slack actually does it.

text: In Slack, the client first gets its token and connection details from the web app backend, then opens a WebSocket to the nearest edge region. There an Envoy proxy forwards it to a Gateway Server, which loads the user's channels and subscribes to them.
why: Real-world counterpart of the 'where do I connect?' balancer service.

text: Slack terminates WebSocket connections on proxies in multiple regions close to users (HAProxy, replaced globally by Envoy) and forwards them to its backend WebSocket services.
why: Shows the load-balancer-in-front option as chosen by the case-study company.

text: Kafka can authenticate client connections (SSL or SASL) and authorise read/write operations per client. An edge server can therefore get a credential limited to writing one topic, so a breach exposes as little as possible.
why: Turns 'only a Kafka connection string' into a concrete least-privilege setup.

text: OWASP classes this as broken access control: users acting outside their intended permissions, e.g. by tampering with a request parameter. The recommended baseline is 'except for public resources, deny by default', so membership must be checked server-side.
why: Gives the correct term and the standard defence.

text: The most common DDoS attacks (UDP reflection, SYN floods) are infrastructure-layer floods. Mitigating them requires network capacity that scales faster than the attack, to filter or absorb it, which an application rate limiter cannot provide.
why: Limits the 'rate limiter prevents DDoS' claim to where it actually applies.

text: An L4 load balancer such as AWS NLB picks a target by flow hash, and 'each individual TCP connection is routed to a single target for the life of the connection'. A WebSocket through it is therefore pinned to one server without terminating the connection at the load balancer.
why: Clarifies how stickiness works at L4 versus L7.

text: WebTransport sends data over HTTP/3 with multiple streams, unidirectional streams and unreliable UDP-like datagrams. MDN lists it as Baseline 2026, working across the latest major browsers since March 2026 (checked 2026-10-12).
why: Answers the student's question with the current status of the alternative.
